When a *path operation function* is declared with plain `def` instead of `async def`, FastAPI runs it in an external threadpool that is then awaited, rather than calling it directly — this avoids blocking the server [c1].

No — using plain `def` for trivial compute-only path operation functions does not give a performance gain in FastAPI; the effect would actually be the opposite, since such functions declared with `def` are run in an external threadpool that is then awaited, rather than being called directly. For these cases, it's better to use `async def` unless the function performs blocking I/O. Still, FastAPI will likely be faster than (or at least comparable to) other frameworks in either case [c1].

It happens when each node doesn't have its own separate storage directory, volume, or mount — the WAL files are unavailable because another Qdrant instance is already using the same files. In Kubernetes each node needs its own volume, in Docker its own storage mount or volume, and in direct deployment its own storage directory; the cluster handles sharing data across nodes correctly on its own once this is set up [c1].

You can return a response right away — for example an HTTP 202 "Accepted" — and run the slow file processing as a background task, since operations like processing a file that must go through a slow process don't require the client to wait for completion before receiving the response [c1].

When `BackgroundTasks` is declared at multiple levels — in the path operation function, in a dependency, or in a sub-dependency — FastAPI knows how to reuse the same object, so all the background tasks declared at those different levels are merged together and run in the background after the response is sent [c1].

Celery is the better choice when you need heavy background computation that doesn't need to share memory or variables with the same process, and especially when you need to run tasks across multiple processes or multiple servers. It does come with more complex configuration, requiring a message/job queue manager like RabbitMQ or Redis. If instead you just need to access variables/objects from the same FastAPI app or run small tasks like sending an email notification, `BackgroundTasks` is sufficient [c1].
